s05.slug: MONDAY · 8:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: The RAZR goes while he is still in the lounge with the Greene open on his knee, GINA across the little outside screen, and he is through the door and into the east stairwell with it against his ear before the third ring. His sister doesn’t call at this hour to say hello.

The landing is the one place in Delgado where the signal holds. He shoves the window up its six inches on a night that has finally stopped dripping, wet cement and eucalyptus and a sprinkler going somewhere below, and sits down on the top step.
“Are you alone?” Gina says.
She is whispering. Behind her something roars, level and endless: the fan in the upstairs bathroom on Glenwood Avenue, the only room in that house with a lock on the door.
“I’m in a stairwell.”
“Is that alone?”
“It’s Delgado. Gina. What.”

“Okay. Don’t freak out. It’s handled.” She takes a breath and goes fast, in order, with the footnotes in, as she has told him everything since she could talk. “It’s twenty of twelve here and I’m in the bathroom, so listen. You didn’t text back this morning. Which, fine. So after school I read all the comments, in the basement on the Dell, with Ma and Rosie still at St. Brigid’s and Nonna upstairs in her chair and Dad out in the garage with the radio. There’s like forty. And most of it’s the jacket. There’s a lady who thinks you’re a Teamster and wants to know if you’re single, and about nine people who think you’re a priest.”
“Gina —”
“And then number thirty-one.”
The fan covers whatever her voice does.

“He’s from home. His name has *Y-town* in it, and a three-three-oh. He said he knew whose jacket that was, and then he said convict.” Her voice goes up, and she pulls it down. “And then he said what for. The actual word. Like it was a fun fact.”

Jack’s free hand has found the stair rail, gray steel under years of gray paint, and he looks at it. There is a night he doesn’t think about. He is good at it, and he gets good at it again now, on purpose, with the sprinkler going below him and the dark standing in the window.

“I reported him,” Gina says. “There’s a button. It has a dropdown, spam or offensive or other. I picked other and typed *he’s wrong*, and then I went back and picked offensive too, just in case. But the button takes a day, so I answered him, too. I signed it. *His sister.* So he’d know who he said it in front of.”
“What did you say?”
“I called him a name.” The fan. “A Catholic one. So it doesn’t count.”
“I’m pretty sure it counts.”

“It doesn’t count *count*.” She hurries on, over it. “They took it down at nine. I checked at nine and ten and eleven and then ten after, in case. It’s just the jacket again. None of them even knew it was Danny’s. They were so *sure* about you. You were a Teamster.” Her breath catches on the next part and she runs straight through the catch. “People say stuff, Jack. I know what to do when people say stuff. You say it right back, and you don’t cry till the door’s locked.”
“Gina.”
“It’s the fan. It dries out your eyes.”

The Carhartt is on its hook in 412, where he left it, and he is cold in a way the window doesn’t account for. He wants to be on Glenwood Avenue, in the upstairs hall, on the floor with his back against that door, the way he sat against it the night she was nine and the Browns lost in the last minute. He is a continent from the hall. He has a stair rail and a paperback, and a sister who has just gone brisk.
“You shouldn’t have had to read them,” he says.
“You weren’t going to.”
“I was.”
“You were going to read the first six and make a joke.”
He has one ready. It is a good one, and he puts it away.
“Don’t tell Ma,” Gina says. “She’ll want to know why I was on the Dell, and then she’ll ask Dad something, and then —” She doesn’t finish the then.
“She finds out everything, Gina. Eventually.”
“Not this week.”
“Where is she now?”

“Downstairs doing Rosie’s lunch for tomorrow. She makes it at night so the bread doesn’t go wet.” Under the fan, very faint, a cupboard door shuts, and another: a sound he could pick out of a thousand. “She thinks I’m on the toilet. I’m on the toilet. Technically.”
He lets her have it. It is nearly midnight where she is.
“And Danny, either. He’d want the guy’s name, and what’s he supposed to do with a name in there.”
“I won’t.”

“Okay.” The roar changes pitch; she has switched the phone to the other ear. “Other thing. It’s the second, a week from tomorrow. Candlemas. Danny’s twenty-three.” Jack knows the room he will be twenty-three in, down to the smell of it. “Are you sending him something? Because I’m making him a card, and it has a candle on it, obviously, it’s *Candlemas*, and I need to know if yours is going to be better so I can stop.”
“Mine’s going to be a card.”
“Put it in my envelope. It’s one stamp.”
“You don’t have to —”
“It’s a stamp, Jack.” Beside her the toilet flushes, for cover. “I have to go. Ma’s going to think I have a condition.”
“Gina —”

choices.key: Gina fought a stranger in a comment thread over Danny. You thanked her.
response: On her end there is only the fan. Then, in the voice she used at nine, coming in from the yard with a skinned knee and not saying it hurt: “ok.” Small. “night jack.”
The roar cuts off in the middle of a second, a switch thrown on Glenwood Avenue, and the line is only a line.

choices.key: Gina fought a stranger over Danny. You told her not to fight them for you. She said she wasn’t.
response: “I’m not fighting for *you*,” Gina says. The fan roars on for the length of a held breath. “I’m fighting because he was wrong.”
She doesn’t wait to be argued with. “Night.” The call ends, and the stairwell has the sprinkler back.

choices.key: Gina fought a stranger over Danny and called him a whited sepulchre. You laughed. So did she.
response: The fan, and a pause with a decision in it. “Whited sepulchre,” Gina whispers. “Matthew twenty-three. I looked it up so I’d get it right.”

He laughs out loud in the stairwell, and it goes down the shaft and comes back up. The fan can’t cover hers; she laughs into what he is fairly sure is one of the good towels, the ones with the C. Then, from the foot of the stairs, faint, his father’s voice comes up through the house about the water bill, and she hisses “*Gotta go*,” and the line is empty.

s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — BEHIND THE SCREEN
body: Del Playa is twenty minutes uphill to Ocean Road if you don’t stop, and he doesn’t. At Sol’s the porch light is on over the new swing, which hangs from its two chains with a blanket folded over one arm of it; through the screen door the television makes a blue square on the front-room ceiling, and Tomás, with the whole of his lungs, is telling the pundits what they can do with their panel. Jack doesn’t slow down. Ocean Road, and the hill, and the A-frame coming up out of the dark with the olive tree over the courtyard wall, and at the back of the nave, behind the blue glass, the little light over the closet door.

At the doors he dips his fingers in the font and the water is colder than the night. Mrs. Fitch is at the card table inside, under one lamp, Sunday’s bulletin spread under it, the diocesan clip-art binder open to ANGELS and a pot of rubber cement at her elbow. The clock over the choir loft says twenty past. Mrs. Fitch has seen it too, and writes nothing in the ledger, which is its own sentence.
“Mr. Costigan.” She holds a cut-out dove up to the lamp, finds it wanting, and lays it down. “My granddaughter showed me your picture on the computer.”
“Which —”

“I didn’t ask which.” She finds the next dove. “At my age one stops asking which. I said a Hail Mary for the pair of you last night, and I expect to say one tonight. Tyler Brandt wants to start a novena. I told him a novena requires the consent of the subject, and he has taken it up with Father.” She lifts the plastic wrap off a plate at her elbow and holds it out. “Lemon bars are Sunday. This is Wednesday. You’ll have one anyway.”

“Father has been in there since eight,” she adds, to the dove. “He said, *If Mr. Costigan comes, I am here*, and went in, and I told him it was Wednesday and nobody comes on Wednesday. He said that was the point of Wednesday.”
He has one. It is cold and sharp and exactly as good as Sunday’s.

body.text: Her nose lifts a degree toward the Carhartt and comes down again. A second lemon bar arrives on his napkin without comment.

body: The index card on the closet door says KNOCK (GENTLY) in her hand. He knocks gently. On the far side, a string of wooden beads stops clicking against the arm of a chair.

The closet is the closet: the kneeler, the linen screen, the hooks from 1962, the Prodigal Son tacked up inside the door at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes, the father already running. Out at the card table Mrs. Fitch has begun to cut, steadily, a good deal louder than a dove requires.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been eleven days since my last confession.”
“Eleven days.” Osei says it back to him. “You are twenty minutes late, and I have said a great deal of the rosary. In Kumasi we say the one who arrives late has at least set out. Tell me.”

He tells it in the order it happened, in the words a Catholic uses, which are short. He keeps the verbs honest, as he has since December: *I went*, and *I stayed*, and *I let it*, never *it happened*. The Saturday night of the sixteenth, straight from this closet to her room. Friday afternoon, in the daylight, with the blind up: everything but the one thing.
Saturday night, in a car at Pismo, where he stopped keeping count and a gearshift stopped him.

Monday at noon, her room, an hour before a seminar: he went up her stairs meaning to, and on her mattress he would have, and he wasn’t the one who stopped it. And that his mother found out from a picture, and asked him one question, and he said *tomorrow*, and through the wall his grandmother said the rosary, loud enough to come down the line, and here it is.

“That’s all of it, Father.” And because it is true, and he has been carrying it since the walk up: “I knew when I went that I’d be in here tonight.” And because that sounds like the worst of it, and isn’t, he gives Osei the rest. “It’s not that I don’t care what it is. I do. I think she’s the answer, Father.”
The scissors stop. The church is quiet to the altar lamp, and the chair on the far side of the screen takes the leg, and Osei is quiet longer than he has ever been quiet in here.
“You think she is the answer,” Osei says at last. “To what question?”

He has two of them in his pocket. He has had them since Christmas, his grandmother’s over her beads and his brother’s across a steel table, and he opens his mouth on the linen to give Osei one, and finds the place in the sentence where it would go, and nothing comes to stand in it.
Osei lets the nothing sit there long enough for both of them to hear it.

“Then find the question,” he says, “before you hand anyone the answer.” The beads move once. “And on the walk home, notice this, because you told it to me yourself: on Monday it was she who kept your Sunday, and not you.”

“You have brought me this same Friday before, my friend, with another date on it. The door will be open next Friday, and God is not tired of you. But the screen is linen, Jack. It is not a curtain you draw between one Friday and the next.” The chair. “In Kumasi, when a man came back every week with the same broken wrist, we did not set it harder. We asked about the staircase.”
“Your mother asked you the right question. Most mothers ask the wrong one.”

Jack looks at the picture on the door, because it is at his eyes: the father with his robe gathered up, running, and a long way down the road the son, small, with his head down. The chair has stopped creaking. “When you leave here,” Osei says, “what is different?”

choices.text: “I want to. I don’t know if I can.”
choices.key: In the closet you told Father Osei you want to change and don’t know if you can. He said that’s further than wanting to want.
response: “I want to,” Jack says. “I don’t know if I can.”
His forehead is nearly on the linen, which smells of starch and old incense and, faintly, of Osei’s soap, and moves a little when Osei leans toward it.

“On the Saturday before last you told me you wanted to want to.” The chair takes the leg, and something comes into the voice behind the linen that, in a less careful man, might be relief. “Wanting is further than wanting to want. It is not far. It is further.” A breath. “A man who wants to, and does not yet know if he can, is standing where the help gets in. Stay there.”

choices.text: “I’ll keep the line. I can’t promise more and mean it.”
choices.key: In the closet you promised Father Osei only what you could mean: the line. He told you to mean it on Friday.
response: “I’ll keep the line,” Jack says. “I can’t promise more and mean it.”
It is the most he has, and he has put all of it on the kneeler where it can be looked at. On the far side the beads move once through a hand.

“Then promise what you can mean,” Osei says, “and mean it on Friday, when it costs something. Tonight it is free. The church is empty, and the screen is linen, and everyone who ever swore anything to me in here swore it easily.” The chair. “Keep the line. I will thank God for every night you keep it. But a line is where you stop. It does not tell you where to walk.”

choices.key: In the closet you asked Father Osei to tell you what to do. He wouldn’t. He said you’d keep it better if it was yours.
response: He hears how it sounds as it leaves him, and leaves it there.

“No.” It isn’t unkind. “You will keep it better if it is yours. Whatever I handed you tonight, you would resent by Friday, and you would be right to.” The beads click once against the chair, and are still. “I will tell you one small thing, though. After the absolution.”

s15a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight.

body: “For your penance,” Osei says, “today’s Gospel. The Sower. You were not at the twelve-ten; I read it to the usual people and Mrs. Fitch.” The chair takes the leg. “Read it tonight, slowly. Stay with the thorns, the part about what chokes it. The seed is strong. The ground is crowded.”

He says the Act of Contrition. It goes as it has gone since he was seven, as far as the last line, *and to avoid the near occasion of sin*, and there he slows down and says each word, because Osei isn’t going to hurry him and the father on the inside of the door is still running.
Behind the linen the shadow of a hand comes up. Osei says all of it this time, every word, in the voice that belongs to the altar and to nothing else.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”
“Thanks be to God.”
“Jack.” Beads, and a breath.

body.text: “You asked me to tell you what to do, and I said no. This is small, and it is not a penance, so you may refuse it.”
body.else: “This is not a penance, so you may refuse it.”

body: “Go home tonight. To your own bed.”
“Yes, Father,” Jack says, not sure yet what he has agreed to.

He comes out of the closet with his knees stiff from the kneeler. In the nave two red cups are lit at the Marian shrine, a long way down the aisle, and the whole church smells of lemon oil and wax and the end of a day.

Mrs. Fitch has gone, and her lamp with her. On the card table, under the plastic wrap, a single lemon bar waits on a napkin with a Post-it on it in her hand: *Mr. Costigan — for the walk.* He takes it.

On the front steps the A-frame is black at his back and the moon stands high over the Channel, nearly full, and Ocean Road is empty both ways: Delgado up the hill to the left, Del Playa down the hill to the right. The RAZR is in his pocket, off since the dog’s bowl. He doesn’t turn it on.

choices.key: After confession Father Osei told you to go home. You went home.
response: He turns up the hill, with the Sower going in his head without its words yet. He will need the book.

choices.key: After confession Father Osei told you to go home. You went to Del Playa.
response: He turns down the hill. He tells himself he is going to tell her where he has been, and that is true, and it isn’t why.
